figures.title: Two ranks, 17.5 GB each, 64 all-reduces per forward pass
figures.caption: Tensor parallelism splits every weight matrix rather than splitting the layer stack, so each rank holds 35 GB ÷ 2 = 17.5 GB and reads only its own half per decode step. Each transformer layer crosses the split twice, after the attention output projection and after the MLP down-projection, so 32 layers need 2 × 32 = 64 all-reduces per forward pass. The residual stream stays local to each rank; only the partial activation crosses the cable.
figures.alt: A five-stage lane. Stage one is the 17.5 GB weight shard held by each rank. Stage two is a transformer block on one rank. Stage three is an all-reduce across the cable. Stage four is the next block. Stage five produces logits. A bypass lane labelled residual stream runs above every stage, showing that the residual connection never leaves the rank.

data.note: The split is by matrix, not by layer, so each rank reads 17.5 GB per decode step rather than 35 GB. What the split buys is capacity; what it costs is 2 × 32 = 64 collectives per forward pass, each of which blocks both ranks until the partial sums land. At decode the batch is small and the payload is small, so the cost is latency. At prefill the payload grows with the prompt and the collective becomes a bandwidth problem of its own.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to walk one forward pass across the pair.

steps.label: A 70B model at four bits is 35 GB of weights. Tensor parallelism splits each matrix by row or column, so each rank holds half of every matrix rather than half of the layers: 35 GB ÷ 2 = 17.5 GB per rank.
Each rank runs the attention half of the block on its own shard and reads only its own 17.5 GB per decode step; neither rank reads the other's half.
After the attention output projection the two partial activations are summed across the cable by an all-reduce in bf16, and both ranks block until the partial sums land.

The MLP down-projection needs the same agreement, so a model with 32 layers runs 2 × 32 = 64 all-reduces per forward pass. At decode the payload is small and the cost is latency; at prefill it grows with the prompt and becomes a bandwidth problem of its own.
The last block emits logits from the sharded output projection. The step is one read of half the weights plus 64 waits, and no roofline contains those waits.

figures.title: The pair's aggregate roof is 31.2 tokens per second against 95.7 on one H100
figures.caption: Bandwidth sets the roof. One rank reads 17.5 GB per step at 273 GB/s, so its ceiling is 273 ÷ 17.5 = 15.6 tokens per second, and two ranks together give 2 × 15.6 = 31.2. A single H100 reads 35 GB at 3,350 GB/s for 3,350 ÷ 35 = 95.7 tokens per second, which is 95.7 ÷ 31.2 = 3.07 times the pair's aggregate. The pair's figure is an upper bound: it assumes the 64 collectives per forward pass are free.
figures.alt: Three horizontal bars in tokens per second. One rank at 15.6. The pair's aggregate at 31.2, marked as the accent bar. One H100 at 95.7, roughly three times the pair.

data.group: batch-one decode roof, bytes over bandwidth
data.note: Every bar is weights divided by bandwidth: 273 ÷ 17.5 = 15.6, 2 × 15.6 = 31.2, and 3,350 ÷ 35 = 95.7. None of the three is a measurement. The pair's bar ignores the collectives, the KV cache re-read per stream, and the fraction of peak bandwidth a real kernel reaches, so the achievable rate sits below 31.2.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to build the pair's roof from bandwidth and weights.

steps.label: One box moves 273 GB/s and holds a coherent 128 GB pool, against the H100's 3,350 GB/s: 3,350 ÷ 273 = 12.3 times the bandwidth.
One rank reads its 17.5 GB shard at 273 GB/s, so 273 ÷ 17.5 = 15.6 tokens per second is its ceiling.
Two ranks each produce tokens, so the aggregate roof is 2 × 15.6 = 31.2 tokens per second, provided the collectives are free. They are not free, so this is an upper bound.
One H100 reads all 35 GB at 3,350 GB/s for 95.7 tokens per second, and 95.7 ÷ 31.2 = 3.07. None of the three bars is a measurement, and none includes the KV cache or the 64 waits.

sources.note: NVIDIA DGX Spark hardware guide: 273 GB/s LPDDR5X unified memory shared between CPU and GPU, in a 128 GB coherent pool per GB10 box. The chapter's 17.5, 15.6 and 31.2 figures are derived from this rate and from a 35 GB four-bit 70B model, not measured.
